summary: Accepted ADR selecting AGPL-3.0-or-later for the whole repo to keep code genuinely open while preventing closed commercial exploitation. Context forced the choice because openness and anti-enclosure pull against each other under a permissive license. Decision allows the copyright holder to sell commercial licenses to parties who cannot comply with AGPL, following Grafana, Qt, and pre-SSPL MongoDB dual-licensing. Why AGPL fits: OSI-approved open source without source-available stigma; forks and hosted services must publish complete source under same terms so commercial actors stay away or negotiate; copyright holder is not bound by their own license for other closed projects. Rejected PolyForm-NC FSL BUSL as source-available, MIT Apache as allowing closed forks, and MIT core plus AGPL app as weaker where it matters most though revisitable. Consequences: LICENSE verbatim AGPL text, LICENSING.md plain explanation and commercial contact, license audit fails build on copyleft restricted deps, no CLA is a live constraint so outside contributions cannot merge without forfeiting commercial dual-license option, no per-file SPDX headers.

sections.title: Context
sections.summary: The project needed a license that keeps the code genuinely open and usable by anyone while preventing a third party from closing it up and selling it. Those two goals pull against each other under a permissive license, which forced a deliberate decision rather than a default choice.

sections.title: Decision
sections.summary: AGPL-3.0-or-later applies to the whole repository. The copyright holder retains the right to sell commercial licenses to anyone who cannot or will not comply with the AGPL. This dual-licensing model is the same pattern Grafana, Qt, and pre-SSPL MongoDB used for open core plus commercial terms.

sections.title: Why AGPL fits
sections.summary: AGPL is a real OSI-approved open-source license without source-available stigma. It prevents closed commercial exploitation in practice because any fork or hosted service must publish its complete source under the same terms, which commercial actors rarely accept; they either stay away or negotiate a separate license. The copyright holder is not bound by their own license, so the same code can still be used in their other closed projects.
topics: holder not bound by own license

sections.title: Rejected alternatives
sections.summary: PolyForm-NC, FSL, and BUSL are closer to the literal anti-commercial requirement but are source-available rather than open source and invite community suspicion this choice exists to avoid. MIT and Apache allow closed commercial forks outright. MIT core plus AGPL app is a cleaner engine adoption story but weakens the guarantee where it matters most; revisitable per-package later because relicensing toward MIT stays open to the copyright holder while the reverse is not.

sections.title: Consequences
sections.summary: LICENSE carries verbatim AGPL-3.0 text; LICENSING.md explains it in plain terms and carries the commercial contact. bun run license:audit fails the build if a copyleft or restricted dependency is introduced. No CLA is in place and this is a live constraint: dual licensing depends on the copyright holder owning all code; the first merged outside contribution without a contributor agreement ends that option. Until a CLA exists, outside contributions cannot be merged without forfeiting commercial licensing. Per-file SPDX headers were considered and are not adopted; the repo-level LICENSE governs.
